title: CELPIP General Listening — Practice Test 12
instructions: Listen to the audio for each part and answer the questions. Each audio plays once.

parts.title: Problem Solving
parts.description: A conversation in which one person has a problem and seeks help from another.

parts.title: Daily Life Conversation
parts.description: An everyday conversation between two people.

parts.title: Listening for Information
parts.description: An informational talk; listen for specific details.

parts.title: Discussion
parts.description: A discussion among people with different viewpoints.

parts.title: Viewpoints
parts.description: A longer talk presenting one speaker's opinion and reasons.

listeningScripts.title: A Parcel Marked Delivered
listeningScripts.text: Caller: Hi. I have a parcel that shows as delivered on your tracking page, but it isn't here. Agent: I'm sorry about that. Do you have the tracking number? Caller: Yes. R-J-four-eight-one-two-Q. Agent: Thank you. I'm seeing it marked delivered at eleven forty on Tuesday, left in a safe place. Does that sound right? Caller: Nobody was home at eleven forty, and we don't have a safe place. There's no porch, and the side gate is locked. Agent: The driver's note says left with neighbour. It doesn't say which one. Caller: That would have been useful. I've asked both sides and neither of them has it. Agent: Then I'll open a missing parcel case. One thing to check before I do. Sometimes a parcel is scanned as delivered at the end of a round and actually goes out the following morning. So if it hasn't turned up by tomorrow evening, the case stands. Caller: And if it does turn up, do I need to call you back? Agent: No. The case closes itself if the parcel scans as delivered again. Caller: What happens if it doesn't turn up at all? Agent: The investigation takes five working days. If we can't locate it, the claim goes to the sender rather than to you, because they are our contract holder. They would either refund you or send a replacement, and which of those happens is their decision, not ours. Caller: So I should tell the shop as well. Agent: I'd tell them today. They can start their side of it at the same time as ours. One last thing — was the parcel worth more than a hundred dollars? Caller: Eighty. Agent: Then the standard cover applies and there's no extra form to fill in.

listeningScripts.title: A Leaving Gift for a Colleague
listeningScripts.text: A: Has anyone said anything about a card for Priya? Friday is her last day. B: I was about to ask you the same thing. I don't think anyone has started one. A: Then it's us. What are people putting in? B: Ten each. Twenty feels like a lot to ask of the people who have only worked with her a month. A: Ten, and nobody has to say what they gave. I'll do the envelope. B: There are twenty-six of us, so if two thirds pay in we are looking at about a hundred and seventy. A: What do you buy someone who is moving to Halifax? B: Not a plant. She's driving, and it's three days. A: Something for the car, then. Or a voucher. B: A voucher is what you buy when you have given up. Let me think. She has talked about that pottery place near the new flat for months. A: A class, then. Can you book a class for somebody who hasn't moved yet? B: You can buy the credit. It doesn't expire for a year. A: Do it. I'll get the card round tomorrow morning, before the ten o'clock meeting, because after that half the floor is in workshops all afternoon. B: Send it the back way. She sits by the printer.

listeningScripts.title: Food Bank Volunteer Briefing
listeningScripts.text: Thanks for coming in. This is the short version of the briefing. The long one is in the handbook, which is on the shelf by the door, and which you should take home with you. Shifts are three hours, and there are two a day: nine to twelve, and one to four. If you can only manage one shift a month, that is genuinely fine. What we do ask is that you tell us by the Thursday before if you cannot come, because the Friday sort is where we allocate people to the week ahead. When you arrive, sign in on the tablet by the entrance, not on the paper sheet. The paper sheet is for deliveries. If the tablet has gone to sleep, the code is the one you were given today. On the floor, the rule that matters most is this. Check every date. Tinned goods we accept up to a year past the best-before, because best-before is a quality date. Anything marked use-by we do not accept past the date at all, however good it looks, because that is a safety date. The difference between those two is the single thing new volunteers most often get wrong. Damaged packaging goes in the blue crate for us to assess. Please don't make that decision yourself. Glass that has broken in transit goes straight in the bin by the loading door, and tell a supervisor, because we log every one. Last thing. If somebody comes to the door during your shift and asks for a hamper, do not turn them away, and do not hand one over either. Take them to the desk at the front. Every hamper goes through an intake conversation, and that conversation is not a formality. It is how we find out that somebody needs a bus ticket or a phone call as well as food.

listeningScripts.title: Yukon Highway Bridge to Be Replaced
listeningScripts.text: The territorial government has confirmed that the bridge on the North Klondike Highway will be replaced rather than repaired, ending two years of argument over which would be cheaper. Engineers found corrosion in the steel supports during an inspection last spring, and the bridge has carried a fifteen-tonne weight limit ever since. That limit has pushed ore trucks onto a detour of a hundred and ten kilometres. The replacement will cost forty-two million dollars and take three summers, because the work can only be done between May and September. During construction, a single-lane temporary crossing will carry traffic, with waits of up to twenty minutes at peak times. The mining association welcomed the decision, but said the temporary crossing must be able to take the weight of a fully loaded truck, or the detour simply continues in practice. The department has confirmed that it will. A community meeting on the construction schedule is set for the ninth of next month.

listeningScripts.title: A Charge for Green-Bin Collection
listeningScripts.text: Pham: The green bin is the only collection we do not charge for. The proposal is forty dollars a year per household, which covers about a third of what the programme costs. Landry: And the households that compost most pay exactly what the ones that put the bin out twice a year pay. That is the part I cannot defend to my members. Ek: We did look at charging by weight. The trucks can weigh a bin. But fitting the fleet came to one point eight million, and then there is the billing system on top. It eats four years of the revenue before it pays for anything at all. Landry: Then charge by bin size. You already offer three sizes. Ek: We do, and that one I could do this year. It is a sticker and a route note, essentially. Pham: My worry with charging by size is what people do with the difference. If the small bin is twenty dollars and the large one is sixty, some of what would have gone in the large bin goes in the black bin instead, and landfill costs us more per tonne than composting does. Landry: Then make the smallest bin free. Nobody has a reason to switch to landfill if the cheapest option costs nothing. Ek: If the smallest is free, I would expect a lot of households to take a small bin and overfill it. An overfilled green bin is a contamination problem, not just a volume one. The lids have to close. Pham: What if the first bin is free and a second one costs? Landry: That I could take to my members. Ek: It is workable. I would want a year of data before we set the price of the second bin.

listeningScripts.title: Publishing Salary Ranges in Job Advertisements
listeningScripts.text: Several provinces and states now require an employer to publish a pay range in the advertisement itself. I have spent some time with the evidence on what actually happens next, and it is more interesting than either side's slogans. Start with what the rule does not do. It does not close the pay gap. The gap does narrow in the studies, but by something in the order of two per cent, not twenty, and mostly by pulling the top of the range down rather than lifting the bottom up. If your argument for the policy is that it makes low earners better paid, the evidence will not carry you there. What it does do, reliably, is save time. Applicants who would have withdrawn at the offer stage withdraw before applying instead. One study found roughly a fifth fewer applications per posting, and no drop at all in the number of hires — which tells you the applications that disappeared were the ones that were never going to end in a job. That is a real gain, and it lands mostly on applicants, who spend hours they cannot bill. The complaint I take most seriously is not the one from employers. It comes from the managers of existing staff. Publishing a range for a new hire tells everybody already doing that job what the company thinks the work is worth now, and if the market has moved, that conversation arrives whether the manager is ready for it or not. The firms that handled this well did the internal review first and advertised second. The firms that did it the other way round spent the following quarter answering questions they had not prepared for. So my position is this. Support the rule, but for the right reason. It is a transparency measure that saves applicants wasted effort and forces employers to face a conversation they were already overdue. Sell it as a fix for the pay gap and you will be held to a result it does not deliver.

questions.prompt: Why is the caller telephoning?
options: A parcel was delivered to the wrong address entirely
A parcel arrived damaged and needs collecting
The tracking page has stopped updating
A parcel is shown as delivered but has not arrived
questions.correctAnswer: A parcel is shown as delivered but has not arrived
questions.explanation: The caller opens by saying the tracking page shows the parcel as delivered although it is not there. Nobody being home is a detail within that, not the reason for the call.

questions.prompt: What does the driver's note say?
options: The parcel was left at the side gate
The parcel was left with a neighbour, without saying which one
The parcel was returned to the depot
The customer signed for the parcel
questions.correctAnswer: The parcel was left with a neighbour, without saying which one
questions.explanation: The agent reads the note as left with neighbour and says it does not identify which one — which is why the caller has already asked both sides.

questions.prompt: Why does the agent suggest waiting until tomorrow evening?
options: A parcel scanned at the end of a round sometimes goes out the next morning
Neighbours are often out during the day
The tracking page updates once every 24 hours
A case cannot be opened until 48 hours have passed
questions.correctAnswer: A parcel scanned at the end of a round sometimes goes out the next morning
questions.explanation: The agent explains that an end-of-round scan can precede the actual delivery by a morning, so the case only stands if nothing arrives by tomorrow evening.

questions.prompt: What does the caller have to do if the parcel arrives?
options: Call to withdraw the case within five days
Confirm receipt in writing to the sender
Nothing, because the case closes on its own
Sign for it on the driver's next visit
questions.correctAnswer: Nothing, because the case closes on its own
questions.explanation: The agent says explicitly that no call back is needed: the case closes itself once the parcel scans as delivered again.

questions.prompt: How long does the investigation take?
options: Twenty-four hours
Until tomorrow evening
Ten working days
Five working days
questions.correctAnswer: Five working days
questions.explanation: The agent gives five working days for the investigation. Tomorrow evening is when the case becomes live, which is a different point in the process.

questions.prompt: Who would the claim be paid to?
options: The sender, because they hold the contract
The caller, as the person expecting the parcel
The neighbour who accepted the parcel
Whoever paid for the postage at the counter
questions.correctAnswer: The sender, because they hold the contract
questions.explanation: The agent says the claim goes to the sender rather than the caller, because the sender is the courier's contract holder, and the sender then decides between a refund and a replacement.

questions.prompt: What does the agent advise the caller to do today?
options: Wait for the courier to contact the shop
Put the complaint in writing to the depot
Tell the shop so it can begin its own side of the claim
Ask the neighbours to check again in the morning
questions.correctAnswer: Tell the shop so it can begin its own side of the claim
questions.explanation: The agent advises telling the shop today so that both sides of the claim run at the same time.

questions.prompt: Why is no extra form needed?
options: The sender has already filed a claim
The parcel was worth less than a hundred dollars
The parcel was sent by a tracked service
The caller reported the loss within a week
questions.correctAnswer: The parcel was worth less than a hundred dollars
questions.explanation: The agent asks whether the value was above a hundred dollars; at eighty, the standard cover applies and no extra form is required.

questions.prompt: Why are the two of them organising this?
options: They were asked to by their manager
They are Priya's closest colleagues
Nobody else appears to have started a card
The usual organiser is away this week
questions.correctAnswer: Nobody else appears to have started a card
questions.explanation: Both say they were about to ask the other, and neither thinks anyone has started one, so A concludes it falls to them.

questions.prompt: How much do they decide to ask for?
options: Ten each
Twenty each
Whatever each person can spare
A hundred and seventy in total
questions.correctAnswer: Ten each
questions.explanation: B suggests ten each rather than twenty, because twenty is a lot to ask of people who have known Priya a month. The hundred and seventy is the total they expect if two thirds contribute.

questions.prompt: Why does B rule out a plant?
options: Priya's new flat has no window space
Plants are what everyone gives
Priya has said she does not like them
Priya has a three-day drive ahead of her
questions.correctAnswer: Priya has a three-day drive ahead of her
questions.explanation: B rejects the plant because Priya is driving to Halifax and the journey takes three days.

questions.prompt: What do they decide to buy?
options: A voucher she can spend anywhere
Credit towards a pottery class
Something useful for the car
A gift chosen once she has moved
questions.correctAnswer: Credit towards a pottery class
questions.explanation: B remembers the pottery place near her new flat, and the credit can be bought now because it does not expire for a year. The voucher is explicitly rejected.

questions.prompt: Why must the card go round before ten o'clock?
options: Priya leaves at lunchtime on Friday
The envelope has to reach the shop by noon
The meeting is where the gift will be presented
Much of the floor will be in workshops that afternoon
questions.correctAnswer: Much of the floor will be in workshops that afternoon
questions.explanation: A wants the card round before the ten o'clock meeting, because after it half the floor is in workshops for the rest of the afternoon.

questions.prompt: How long is a single shift?
options: Three hours
Two hours
A full morning and afternoon
It depends on the day
questions.correctAnswer: Three hours
questions.explanation: Shifts are three hours, and there are two of them a day: nine to twelve and one to four.

questions.prompt: By when must volunteers report that they cannot come?
options: The Friday before
Twenty-four hours ahead
The Thursday before
The start of the month
questions.correctAnswer: The Thursday before
questions.explanation: Absences must be reported by the Thursday before, because the Friday sort is when people are allocated to the week ahead.

questions.prompt: What is the paper sheet used for?
options: Volunteers whose shift has been swapped
Deliveries
Signing in when the tablet is asleep
Recording damaged packaging
questions.correctAnswer: Deliveries
questions.explanation: Volunteers sign in on the tablet; the paper sheet is for deliveries. If the tablet is asleep, the answer is the code, not the paper sheet.

questions.prompt: What is the rule for tinned goods past a best-before date?
options: They are accepted only if the tin is undamaged
They are refused like anything else past its date
They go in the blue crate to be assessed
They are accepted for up to a year afterwards
questions.correctAnswer: They are accepted for up to a year afterwards
questions.explanation: Tinned goods are accepted up to a year past the best-before, because best-before is a quality date rather than a safety one.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say new volunteers most often get wrong?
options: The difference between a best-before date and a use-by date
Which crate damaged packaging belongs in
Signing in on the wrong sheet
How long a shift lasts
questions.correctAnswer: The difference between a best-before date and a use-by date
questions.explanation: The speaker names the best-before and use-by distinction as the single thing new volunteers most often get wrong: one is quality, the other safety.

questions.prompt: What should a volunteer do if someone asks for a hamper?
options: Hand one over and record it afterwards
Explain that hampers are booked in advance
Take the person to the desk at the front
Fetch a supervisor to the door
questions.correctAnswer: Take the person to the desk at the front
questions.explanation: Volunteers must neither refuse nor hand one over, but take the person to the front desk, because every hamper goes through an intake conversation that may surface other needs.

questions.prompt: What has the government decided?
options: The bridge will be repaired and its weight limit lifted
The bridge will be replaced rather than repaired
The bridge will close and traffic will use the detour
A second bridge will be built alongside the first
questions.correctAnswer: The bridge will be replaced rather than repaired
questions.explanation: The decision is replacement rather than repair, which ends a two-year argument about which would cost less.

questions.prompt: Why was the weight limit imposed?
options: Traffic had grown beyond the bridge's design
The detour route needed the heavier vehicles
An ore truck damaged the deck last spring
Corrosion was found in the steel supports
questions.correctAnswer: Corrosion was found in the steel supports
questions.explanation: An inspection last spring found corrosion in the steel supports, and the fifteen-tonne limit has been in place since.

questions.prompt: Why will the work take three summers?
options: The budget is released one year at a time
The temporary crossing must be built first
The work can only be carried out from May to September
Only one contractor is available in the territory
questions.correctAnswer: The work can only be carried out from May to September
questions.explanation: Construction is confined to May through September, which is why a forty-two-million-dollar job stretches across three summers.

questions.prompt: What did the mining association insist on?
options: That the temporary crossing carry a fully loaded truck
That the detour be paved before construction starts
That waits be kept under twenty minutes
That the replacement be finished in two summers
questions.correctAnswer: That the temporary crossing carry a fully loaded truck
questions.explanation: The association welcomed the decision but said the temporary crossing must take the weight of a fully loaded truck, or the detour continues in practice. The department confirmed it will.

questions.prompt: What is happening on the ninth of next month?
options: The weight limit is lifted
A community meeting about the construction schedule
Construction begins on the temporary crossing
The department publishes its final costs
questions.correctAnswer: A community meeting about the construction schedule
questions.explanation: A community meeting on the construction schedule is set for the ninth of next month.

questions.prompt: What is Pham proposing?
options: A charge based on the weight each household puts out
Ending green-bin collection for households that rarely use it
Raising the existing green-bin charge by forty dollars
A flat yearly charge of forty dollars a household
questions.correctAnswer: A flat yearly charge of forty dollars a household
questions.explanation: Pham's proposal is forty dollars a year per household — the green bin being the only collection not currently charged for — covering about a third of the programme's cost.

questions.prompt: What is Landry's objection to it?
options: Households that compost little would pay the same as those that compost a lot
Forty dollars is more than most households can afford
The charge covers only a third of the cost
Her members were not consulted before the proposal
questions.correctAnswer: Households that compost little would pay the same as those that compost a lot
questions.explanation: Landry's objection is that a flat charge treats a household using the bin twice a year identically to one composting heavily, which she cannot defend to her members.

questions.prompt: Why was charging by weight rejected?
options: The trucks are not able to weigh a bin
Residents objected to being weighed
Fitting the trucks would swallow several years of the revenue
The billing system already exists for other collections
questions.correctAnswer: Fitting the trucks would swallow several years of the revenue
questions.explanation: Ek says the trucks can weigh a bin, but fitting the fleet costs one point eight million plus a billing system, eating four years of revenue before returning anything.

questions.prompt: What does Ek say could be done this year?
options: Fitting weighing equipment to part of the fleet
Charging according to the size of the bin
Making the smallest bin free of charge
Collecting a year of data on bin use
questions.correctAnswer: Charging according to the size of the bin
questions.explanation: Ek says charging by size is possible this year, since the city already offers three sizes and it amounts to a sticker and a route note.

questions.prompt: What is Pham's worry about charging by size?
options: Waste would be moved into the black bin, which costs more to dispose of
Households would refuse to pay for the larger bins
The three sizes are too similar to matter
Bin sizes would have to be checked every week
questions.correctAnswer: Waste would be moved into the black bin, which costs more to dispose of
questions.explanation: Pham's worry is the difference in price pushing material into the black bin, and landfill costing the city more per tonne than composting.

questions.prompt: Why does Ek resist making the smallest bin free?
options: The revenue would not cover the programme
Small bins are the most expensive to collect
Free collection encourages people to compost less
Households would take a small bin and overfill it
questions.correctAnswer: Households would take a small bin and overfill it
questions.explanation: Ek expects households to take the free small bin and overfill it, which is a contamination problem rather than merely a volume one, because the lids have to close.

questions.prompt: What compromise do the three of them reach?
options: A flat charge reduced to twenty dollars
The first bin free, with a charge for a second one
Charging by weight once the fleet is fitted
Delaying any charge until next year
questions.correctAnswer: The first bin free, with a charge for a second one
questions.explanation: Pham suggests a free first bin with a second one charged for; Landry says she could take that to her members and Ek calls it workable.

questions.prompt: What does Ek want before the second-bin price is set?
options: A vote of Landry's members
A trial in one neighbourhood
A year of data
The cost of the billing system
questions.correctAnswer: A year of data
questions.explanation: Ek accepts the compromise but wants a year of data before the price of the second bin is fixed.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say the rule does not achieve?
options: Persuading employers to advertise more posts
Reducing the number of applications received
Closing the pay gap to any meaningful degree
Making job advertisements easier to compare
questions.correctAnswer: Closing the pay gap to any meaningful degree
questions.explanation: The speaker opens the case against by saying the rule does not close the pay gap: it narrows by around two per cent rather than twenty.

questions.prompt: Where the gap does narrow, how does it happen?
options: Mainly by lifting the bottom of the range up
Mainly by pulling the top of the range down
By raising pay across the whole range at once
By narrowing the range advertised in the first place
questions.correctAnswer: Mainly by pulling the top of the range down
questions.explanation: The narrowing happens mostly by pulling the top of the range down rather than lifting the bottom up, which is why the policy does not make low earners better paid.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say the rule reliably does?
options: It raises the quality of the candidates who apply
It reduces the cost of advertising a post
It shortens the time taken to fill a vacancy
It saves applicants time they would have wasted
questions.correctAnswer: It saves applicants time they would have wasted
questions.explanation: The reliable effect is saved time: applicants who would have withdrawn at the offer stage withdraw before applying, and the hours saved are theirs.

questions.prompt: What did the study find about the number of hires?
options: It did not fall, even though applications did
It rose alongside the fall in applications
It fell in proportion with the applications
It was not measured by the study
questions.correctAnswer: It did not fall, even though applications did
questions.explanation: Roughly a fifth fewer applications came in per posting with no drop at all in hires, which is how the speaker knows the lost applications were never going to end in a job.

questions.prompt: Whose complaint does the speaker take most seriously?
options: That of employers advertising the posts
That of applicants who withdraw early
That of managers of existing staff
That of the provinces enforcing the rule
questions.correctAnswer: That of managers of existing staff
questions.explanation: The speaker says the complaint worth taking seriously comes not from employers but from the managers of staff already doing the job, who face a pay conversation on the advertisement's timing rather than their own.

questions.prompt: What distinguished the firms that handled the change well?
options: They reviewed pay internally before advertising
They advertised a narrower range than required
They explained the new rule to staff in advance
They delayed advertising until the following quarter
questions.correctAnswer: They reviewed pay internally before advertising
questions.explanation: Firms that did the internal review first and advertised second handled it well; those that reversed the order spent the next quarter answering questions they had not prepared for.
